content: Participants in the project have the option to opt out of enhanced case reporting if they choose not to participate. However, even if they opt out, they will still receive biomarker testing at no cost. The project involves surveillance activities that utilize data collected during routine clinical care and public health operations. As such, it may or may not require ethics committee clearance. Nonetheless, the project will be submitted to both national and WHO ethics committees to determine whether a full review, expedited review, or an exception is applicable. Future projects implementing these standard operating procedures (SOPs) with financial or technical support from WHO will require subsequent reviews of the national protocol by both the national ethics committee and the WHO ethics committee. Expected Outputs: 1. Identification of trends in acute hepatitis by type, location, age, and sex. 2. Comparative analysis of different types of acute hepatitis, focusing on the proportion of patients exposed to potential risk factors during the incubation period. Expected Outcomes: 1. 2. Surveillance capacity for acute hepatitis will be strengthened, with improved local capacity-building at participating sites. 3. Lessons learned will inform the expansion of the project to additional sites. 4. A collaborative network of clinicians and laboratory specialists will be established, which can support testing, treatment, and biomarker surveys for in-vitro diagnostics. References: The references include technical reports, global health strategies, and studies on hepatitis epidemiology, vaccination, and risk factors. These sources provide a comprehensive foundation for understanding the burden of hepatitis and its implications for public health strategies. Key studies cited include analyses of hepatitis A, B, C, and E infections, their risk factors, and the impact of vaccination programs in various countries. Surveillance Procedures: The surveillance project aims to track acute hepatitis cases in the participating country by identifying the viruses involved and their sources. This information will help prevent hepatitis and assist the Ministry of Health in planning prevention strategies. Participants will be asked questions about their condition, and a blood test will be conducted to determine the type of hepatitis (A, B, C, or E). The data collected will be anonymized and used for surveillance purposes, ensuring confidentiality. Risks and Benefits: The risks associated with the blood test are minimal but may include discomfort, bruising, or infection at the site of blood draw. Discussing personal circumstances during the interview may also cause discomfort. Ethical Considerations: Participants have the right to refuse the use of their data for surveillance purposes. If they choose to opt out, their data will remain confidential and will not be used in the project. This decision will not affect their care or access to test results. Contact Information: Participants can contact the designated project lead or ethics representative for any questions or concerns regarding the surveillance project or its ethical aspects. Case Definitions and Diagnostic Criteria: The WHO surveillance case definitions for viral hepatitis are designed for reporting and surveillance purposes. These definitions include clinical criteria (e.g., symptoms such as jaundice, nausea, and elevated ALT levels) and biomarker or epidemiological criteria for confirmed cases. Specific thresholds and tests are used to differentiate acute from chronic hepatitis and to improve diagnostic specificity. Hepatic Encephalopathy Criteria: The West Haven criteria are used to classify hepatic encephalopathy (HE) into grades based on clinical and neuropsychological findings. These grades range from minimal HE (subtle psychometric changes) to Grade IV (coma). Diagnosis requires that all conditions be related to liver insufficiency or portosystemic shunting.
